props.title: Get Out
props.initialSlug: A black man uncovers a white family's sinister secret

sections.content: Jordan Peele's **Get Out** (2017) masterfully reimagines horror through a racial lens, creating a new subgenre of social thriller. The film's "sunken place" became an instant cultural touchstone, following in the footsteps of psychological horror landmarks like **Rosemary's Baby** (1968) and The Stepford Wives (1975). Peele's directorial debut transforms microaggressions and liberal racism into visceral terror, using genre conventions to expose societal horrors hiding in plain sight.

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through horror, inspiring a wave of socially conscious genre films like Us (2019), Candyman (2021), and **Antebellum** (2020). Like **The Twilight Zone** (1959-1964), which Peele would later reboot, Get Out uses genre elements to tackle pressing social issues. The film's mix of comedy and horror recalls **An American Werewolf in London** (1981), while its exploration of body horror draws from **Invasion of the Body Snatchers** (1956).

The technical mastery in Get Out deserves special attention. Cinematographer Toby Oliver's use of the "sunken place" sequences revolutionized how horror visualizes psychological trauma, comparable to the innovative dream sequences in **A Nightmare on Elm Street** (1984). The film's sound design, particularly in the stirring spoon scene, creates unbearable tension similar to the heightened audio work in **The Silence of the Lambs** (1991). sections.content: Get Out sparked a renaissance in social horror, paving the way for films like **Sorry to Bother You** (2018) and **The Platform** (2019). Its success proved audiences would embrace horror films that tackle complex social issues, similar to how **Dawn of the Dead** (1978) used zombies to critique consumerism. The film's exploration of the Black experience in white spaces shares DNA with non-horror works like **Dear White People** (2014), while maintaining the psychological dread of **The Shining** (1980).
